query: For as-deposited, non-equiatomic FeMnNiGeSi-type high-entropy alloys intended for magnetic refrigeration, what testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain what governs their magnetocaloric response and hysteresis during low-applied-field magnetic-cooling cycles? Earlier work focused mainly on arc-melted ingots and melt-spun microribbons, where an ordered single-phase hexagonal state undergoes a first-order magnetostructural transition that produces a large but sharp and hysteretic entropy change; these bulk forms also have limited heat-exchange rates because of their low surface-to-volume ratio. Prior searches have largely emphasized composition-dependent changes in transition temperature or response amplitude, with most studies pursuing only one optimization variable. Under the constraints of avoiding rare-earth elements, retaining mechanical stability and low cost, enabling rapid heat exchange, and limiting hysteretic losses, specify one controlled intervention that would distinguish the proposed governing explanation from alternatives, the predicted observations relative to the as-deposited baseline, the boundaries over which those predictions should hold, the prior observations that support the hypothesis, and a result that would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: Increasing the surface-to-volume ratio by sputter depositing as-deposited, non-equiatomic FeMnNiGeSi-type high-entropy alloy films onto textured or porous substrates increases the density of interfacial nucleation sites during the first-order magnetostructural transition, which will broaden the transformation kinetics, reduce the hysteretic losses, and enable more efficient magnetocaloric cycling at low applied fields.
generation.material_initial_state: As-deposited, non-equiatomic FeMnNiGeSi-type HEA with an ordered single-phase hexagonal structure forming in bulk (arc-melted or melt-spun forms) that exhibit a sharp, hysteretic first-order magnetostructural transition.
generation.intervention: Sputter deposition of the HEA onto substrates engineered to have a high surface-to-volume ratio via textured or porous structures.
generation.conditions: Low-applied-field magnetic-cooling cycles conducted near the magnetostructural transition temperature, with processing conditions that do not alter the alloy’s composition.
generation.structural_mediator: Enhanced interfacial density and altered grain/nucleation structure in the deposited films compared to bulk forms.
generation.mechanism: The increased surface-to-volume ratio provides additional heterogeneous nucleation sites which distribute the transition over a wider temperature range, thereby reducing the abruptness of the phase transformation and the associated hysteresis while maintaining a large magnetocaloric entropy change.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to the as-deposited bulk baseline, the sputter-deposited films on textured/porous substrates will exhibit a more gradual magnetostructural transition with reduced hysteresis and improved heat exchange efficiency, albeit with some uncertainty in the exact magnitude of these changes.
generation.baseline: Bulk arc-melted ingots or melt-spun microribbons that exhibit a sharp, highly hysteretic magnetostructural transition with low surface area.
generation.boundary: Predictions should hold for non-equiatomic FeMnNiGeSi-type HEAs processed under similar low-field conditions and for deposition methods that reliably enhance surface area without altering the chemical composition or mechanical stability. The effect may vary if processing parameters (e.g., deposition temperature or substrate texture) fall outside the optimized range.
generation.uncertainty: Quantitative details regarding the improvement in heat exchange rates and the exact reduction in hysteresis remain uncertain and depend on the specific microstructural features achieved through deposition.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of films of the non-equiatomic FeMnNiGeSi-type HEA using sputter deposition: one set on textured/porous substrates (high surface-to-volume ratio) and a control set on flat, conventional substrates. Conduct low-field magnetic-cooling cycles around the transition temperature and measure the magnetocaloric response and hysteresis in each sample.
measurements: Magnetization vs. temperature curves during cooling/warming cycles
Magnetic entropy change determined from isothermal magnetization measurements
Direct thermal measurements of heat exchange rates
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the films deposited on textured/porous substrates do not show a statistically significant reduction in hysteresis width and improvement in heat exchange efficiency (or if they exhibit a degraded magnetocaloric response) compared to the control samples, then the hypothesis that the enhanced surface-to-volume ratio mediates improved transformation kinetics via increased interfacial nucleation is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: AbstractInvestigation into non-equiatomic high-entropy alloys has grown in recent years due to questions about the role of entropy stabilization in forming single-phase solid solutions. Non-equiatomic alloys have been shown to retain the outstanding mechanical properties exhibited by their equiatomic counterparts and even improve electrical, thermal, and magnetic properties, albeit with relaxed composition bounds. However, much remains to understand the processing–structure–property relationships in all classes of so-called high-entropy alloys (HEAs). Here, we are motivated by the natural phenomena of crystal growth and equilibrium conditions to introduce a method of HEA development where controlled processing conditions determine the most probable and stable composition. This is demonstrated by cooling an equiatomic CrMnFeCoNiCu alloy from the melt steadily over 3 days (cooling rate ~4 °C/h). The result is an alloy containing large Cr-rich precipitates and an almost Cr-free matrix exhibiting compositions within the MnFeCoNiCu system (with trace amounts of Cr). While these studies demonstrate that the relationship between composition and phase stability in HEAs has certainly been considered, expansion beyond the circumstances around the σ-phase has been limited. The further inclusion of processing conditions—the importance of which has been emphasized earlier—to this equation beyond prolonged annealing has not been presented in the literature. Here, we propose a fabrication method applicable to both equiatomic and non-equiatomic HEAs, where controlled processing conditions determine the most probable and stable composition. This is demonstrated through a thorough experimental analysis that tests the following hypotheses: For HEAs, an equiatomic composition maximizes configurational entropy, but structure and phase stability are not necessarily optimized. CrMnFeCoNi is not the most stable or preferred alloy composition within the CrMnFeCoNiCu system if the processing conditions (especially a slow cooling rate from the melt) are controlled.

The unpredictability of geopolitical tensions and resulting supply chain and pricing instabilities make it imperative to explore rare earth free magnetic materials. As such, we have investigated fully transition metal based “high entropy alloys” in the context of the magnetocaloric effect. We find the NiFeCoCrPdx family exhibits a second order magnetic phase transition whose critical temperature is tunable from 100 K to well above room temperature. The system notably displays changes in the functionality of the magnetic entropy change depending on x, which leads to nearly 40% enhancement of the refrigerant capacity. A detailed statistical analysis of the universal scaling behavior provides direct evidence that heat treatment and Pd additions reduce the distribution of exchange energies in the system, leading to a more magnetically homogeneous alloy. The general implications of this work are that the parent NiFeCoCr compound can be tuned dramatically with FCC metal additives. The so-called “high entropy alloys” (HEAs) are a class of emergent transition metal alloys that hold great potential for advanced manufacturing, and which may impact magnetocalorics. These are near equimolar alloys with high entropy of mixing when in a random solid solution. These materials have been pursued for high hardness and resistance to wear and corrosion, which are attractive properties for a myriad of applications. Fe1Co1Ni1Cr1Pdx is an example HEA system with tunable magnetic properties. The addition of Pd was shown to change the critical temperature (Tc) from 300 to 500 K for x = 1 to 2, along with enhancement of the saturation magnetization; previous works have used high percentages of Pd as a stabilizing agent in similar high strength bulk alloys. In this work, we explore the magnetic properties of the Fe1Co1Ni1Cr1Pdx alloy family, as-rolled and after annealing, with low molar fractions of Pd. We find improvement in the magnetocaloric properties throughout the system. A detailed statistical analysis of the universal scaling behavior suggest this originates predominately from the homogenization of the alloy with both Pd and heat treatment. Most of the studies on magnetic and electrical properties of high entropy alloys focus on equiatomic FeCoCrNiX alloy (i.e., derivatives of the FeCoCrNiMn Cantor alloy) where X is Mn, Ti, Cu, or Pd and non-equiatomic FeCoCrNi with slight doping of Al, Cu, and Si. A wide spectrum of magnetic properties has been reported ranging from soft to semi-soft magnetic behavior in their coercivity. Among these alloys, the most studied single-phase FCC Cantor alloy exhibited multiple magnetic transitions from disordered paramagnetic phase to spin glass and subsequently to an ordered ferromagnetic state at low temperatures. chosen.conditions: as-deposited non-equiatomic FeMnNiGeSi-type high-entropy alloy films fabricated to enhance surface area, tested under low-applied-field magnetic-cooling cycles at near-ambient temperatures
chosen.why: This move directly addresses the performance limitation arising from the low heat-exchange rates in conventional bulk forms by engineering the surface geometry to boost the specific surface area. It distinguishes the controlled mechanistic hypothesis by altering the heat dissipation pathway, thereby clarifying the role of surface effects on the magnetocaloric response and hysteresis—a critical variable overlooked in previous single-variable, composition-focused studies.

frame.system: FeMnNiGeSi-type high-entropy alloys in an as-deposited, non-equiatomic state with an ordered single-phase hexagonal structure that undergo a first-order magnetostructural transition.
frame.goal: To develop a mechanistic hypothesis explaining how microstructural or compositional control influences the balance between a large magnetocaloric effect and hysteresis losses during low-applied-field magnetic-cooling cycles, thereby enabling rapid heat exchange without reliance on rare-earth elements.
frame.limitation: Bulk forms (arc-melted ingots and melt-spun microribbons) show a large but very sharp, hysteretic entropy change and poor heat exchange due to their low surface-to-volume ratio. Additionally, prior work has optimized mainly along a single compositional axis, not addressing multi-variable optimization under critical constraints like mechanical stability, cost, and hysteresis minimization.
root_cause_cues: limited heat-exchange rates because of their low surface-to-volume ratio
frame.regime: Low-applied-field magnetic-cooling cycles near the temperature where the first-order magnetostructural transition occurs, with conditions reflecting the rapid heat transfer but low surface-area configurations.
prior_attempts: Arc-melted ingots and melt-spun microribbons have been investigated, which produced an ordered single-phase hexagonal state undergoing a sharp, hysteretic transition.

Prior studies largely focused on composition-dependent changes (i.e., single optimization variable) rather than exploring alternative controlled interventions to influence the transition kinetics or structural heterogeneities.

decision.trend: Earlier work on rare‐earth‐free, transition‐metal high-entropy alloys for magnetocaloric applications has focused on bulk processing routes (arc-melting, melt-spinning) that produce single-phase hexagonal states with first-order magnetostructural transitions. These studies tuned the transition temperature or the amplitude of the entropy change by varying composition along a single axis, although the sharp nature of the transition and high hysteresis—together with low heat‐exchange rates due to limited surface area—remained problematic.
decision.unsolved: It remains unclear how non‐compositional processing interventions—specifically control of microstructure and enhancement of the surface-to-volume ratio—affect the balance between a large magnetocaloric response and hysteresis losses during low-applied-field cooling cycles. The mechanistic role of interfacial and nucleation dynamics remains untested.
decision.lever: surface-to-volume ratio via sputter deposition on textured/porous substrates
decision.why: By employing a controlled processing experiment where as-deposited FeMnNiGeSi-type HEA films are grown on substrates engineered for high surface area, the experiment directly tests the hypothesis that enhanced interfacial density and altered transformation kinetics can reduce hysteresis and improve heat exchange without changing composition. This approach fills the gap left by earlier work that only varied composition, aligning with the performance limitation niche and using processing parameters as the lever.
